Function-to-taxon visualizations

function-to-taxon.Rmd

Start here when a function is your point of interest. A pooled functional profile may tell you that the community differs, but it does not tell you whether the same taxa contribute in both groups. Function-centered analysis lets us examine those contributors directly.

The figures follow the same principles as the taxon-centered workflow, with the roles reversed. The statistical analysis must also be function-centered. Redrawing a taxon-centered result with the nodes swapped would not answer the same question.

Use the result list fitted with direction = "function"; do not transpose taxon-oriented fitted results. Run the shared setup first. Figures are collected in the stratified demonstration.

Sankey

Use this overview to see which taxa are linked to each selected function. Keeping individual KOs visible makes it easier to follow a specific feature; grouping functions can be useful for a broader summary. Decide which resolution you want before interpreting a visually large group of links.

Functions appear on the left and taxa on the right. Set group_functions = FALSE to retain individual KOs. Optional taxonomy or ASV phylogeny appears on the taxon side.

p_fun_sankey <- fun2tax_sankey(
  result_fun, pathway = "KO", group_functions = FALSE,
  tree_mode = "phylogeny", physeq = ps, phylo_tree = demo$phylo_tree
)
save_sankey(p_fun_sankey, file.path(out, "fun2tax_sankey.html"))
save_sankey(p_fun_sankey, file.path(out, "fun2tax_sankey.pdf"))

Chord

Use Chord to compare the predicted contributions behind the selected relationships. A broad ribbon identifies a large mean contribution in the plotted subset, while the outer bar describes the absolute modeled effect. Neither should be substituted for the other.

The example below narrows the view to one KO. This is often a helpful first step when a full diagram is crowded. Select a function you can interpret, inspect its contributors, then broaden the view if needed.

The contribution weighting, effect colours, taxonomy bands and export interfaces match the taxon-to-function Chord. Use function-oriented results and select relevant function IDs.

hexokinase <- data.frame(
  function_id = "K00844", function_group = "Carbohydrate metabolism",
  function_name = "Hexokinase"
)
p_fun_chord <- fun2tax_chord(
  result_fun, strat_path, ps, group = group_col,
  contrast = c(reference, target), functions = "K00844",
  max_taxa_per_function = 2, function_table = hexokinase, draw = FALSE
)
save_chord(p_fun_chord, file.path(out, "fun2tax_chord.png"))
save_chord(p_fun_chord, file.path(out, "fun2tax_chord.pdf"))

Contribution boxplots

For a selected function, compare how different taxa contribute across sample groups. Look for the spread and overlap as well as the medians. The log-transformed y-axis helps show contributions on different scales; equal visual distances on that axis are not equal changes in the original contribution units.

An ungrouped call returns one named plot per function. The y-axis is log10(contribution + 1e-6).

fun_boxes <- fun2tax_box(
  strat_path, result_fun, ps, group = group_col,
  pathway = "KO", group_functions = FALSE
)
p_fun_box <- fun_boxes[["K00844"]]
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(out, "fun2tax_box.pdf"), p_fun_box,
                width = 9, height = 6)

Association dendrogram

Here the function defines a branch and its contributing taxa define the leaves. This view is useful for comparing which taxa appear among the selected model effects for several functions. It is an association summary, so do not read it as a phylogenetic tree or a clustering of taxon abundance profiles.

Functions label branches, and contributing taxa label the leaves. top_n_per_function controls how many taxa are displayed per function.

p_fun_dendro <- fun2tax_dendro(
  result_fun, top_n_per_function = 3, label_size = 2.6,
  wrap_width = 20
)$plot
p_fun_dendro <- p_fun_dendro +
  ggplot2::coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.6, 1.6), ylim = c(-1.6, 1.6), clip = "off")
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(out, "fun2tax_dendrogram.pdf"), p_fun_dendro,
                width = 10, height = 7.5)

Signed model effects

A signed-effect plot brings the contrast into focus. Which taxa have positive effects for the selected function, and which have negative effects? Read the model scale and reference group before comparing bar lengths, and remember that a large coefficient does not by itself imply the largest absolute contribution.

fun_effects <- fun2tax_logfc(result_fun, top_n = 3)
p_fun_effect <- fun_effects[["K00844"]] +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "MaAsLin2 AST coefficient")
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(out, "fun2tax_effect.pdf"), p_fun_effect,
                width = 8, height = 5)

Choose names from names(result_fun) and record the reference/target contrast. Signed effects are backend-dependent model estimates; MaAsLin2 AST coefficients are not literal log fold changes.

When you return to the community-level result

A function may change overall because a few contributors shift strongly or because many shift together. It may also remain similar in total while its contributors change. Use the function-centered plots to investigate those possibilities, then return to the pooled profile for context. The two levels describe related parts of the same community, rather than identical measurements.
